topic.subject: maths
topic.title: Changing the subject of a formula
topic.scope: Rearranging formulas such as v=u+at, A=πr² and C=2πr; doing the same operation on both sides; undoing operations in reverse order; substituting values before or after rearranging; handling squares and square roots when isolating a variable.

misconceptions.statement: A formula can only be used to find the letter written alone on its left side.
misconceptions.why: Students meet formulas always written as A = ... or v = ... and treat the layout as fixed.
misconceptions.fix: The equals sign works both ways, so any letter can be made the subject by doing the same thing to both sides.

probe.question: Can A = πr² be used to write r in terms of A?
probe.wrong_answer: No, A is on the left so the formula only gives A.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule's written layout is fixed and cannot change

misconceptions.statement: The new subject may still appear on the right side of the rearranged formula.
misconceptions.why: Students stop after one step without checking that the letter is alone.
misconceptions.fix: The subject must be alone on one side, and the other side must not contain it.

probe.question: Make r the subject of A = πr².

misconceptions.root_belief: a procedure is finished once some steps are done

misconceptions.statement: π is a letter that can be cancelled or ignored while rearranging.
misconceptions.why: π looks like a symbol rather than a number, so students drop it.
misconceptions.fix: π is the fixed number about 3.14 and must be divided out like any other multiplier.

probe.question: Make r the subject of C = 2πr.

misconceptions.root_belief: symbols with no visible value can be ignored

misconceptions.statement: You cannot rearrange a formula until you know numbers for the other letters.
misconceptions.why: Early algebra work always ends in a numerical answer, so letters-only answers feel incomplete.
misconceptions.fix: A formula can be rearranged with letters only, and the numbers are put in afterwards if needed.

probe.question: Make t the subject of v = u + at.
probe.wrong_answer: It is not possible without values of v, u and a.

misconceptions.root_belief: an answer must always be a number
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' difficulty accepting algebraic expressions as answers (lack of closure)

misconceptions.statement: You can divide only one side of a formula by a letter and the equals sign still holds.
misconceptions.why: Students treat = as a signal to do something to the right side rather than as a balance.
misconceptions.fix: Whatever is done to one side must be done to the other side to keep the two sides equal.

probe.question: Make b the subject of A = lb.
probe.wrong_answer: b = A (after dividing the right side by l only)

misconceptions.root_belief: equals means 'now give the answer', not balance
misconceptions.source_hint: research on the operational view of the equals sign

misconceptions.statement: Dividing both sides by t means dividing only the term that has t in it.
misconceptions.why: Students apply the operation to the nearest term instead of the whole side.
misconceptions.fix: Every term on each side must be divided, so u + at becomes u/t + a.

probe.question: Divide both sides of v = u + at by t. Write the result.

misconceptions.root_belief: an operation affects only the nearest part
misconceptions.source_hint: research on errors in solving linear equations, such as applying an operation to one term only

misconceptions.statement: When a term moves to the other side it keeps its sign.
misconceptions.why: Students learn 'transposing' as moving a term without understanding it is adding or subtracting.
misconceptions.fix: Moving a term across the equals sign means adding or subtracting it on both sides, so its sign changes.

probe.question: Make at the subject of v = u + at.

misconceptions.root_belief: moving a symbol does not change it
misconceptions.source_hint: research on transposition errors in school algebra

misconceptions.statement: A division can be removed by dividing both sides by the same number again.
misconceptions.why: Students remember 'divide to isolate' and repeat the same operation.
misconceptions.fix: Division is undone by multiplying both sides by the same number.

probe.question: Make y the subject of x = y/5.

misconceptions.root_belief: the same operation again cancels it out
misconceptions.source_hint: research on inverse operations errors in solving equations

misconceptions.statement: A number that multiplies the subject is removed by subtracting it.
misconceptions.why: Students think removing a number means taking it away.
misconceptions.fix: A multiplier is removed by dividing both sides by it.

probe.question: Make r the subject of C = 2πr.

misconceptions.root_belief: a number is removed by taking it away

misconceptions.statement: Operations are undone in the same order in which they appear in the formula.
misconceptions.why: Students read left to right and undo in that order.
misconceptions.fix: Operations are undone in reverse order, last operation done is first one undone.

probe.question: Make C the subject of F = (9/5)C + 32.

misconceptions.root_belief: steps are undone in the order they are written
misconceptions.source_hint: research on order of operations in inverse (working backwards) problems

misconceptions.statement: When the subject has a minus sign, the sign can be dropped and the numerator left as it is.
misconceptions.why: Students treat the minus as part of the working, not the quantity, and avoid negatives.
misconceptions.fix: If -at = v - u, divide by -a (or multiply by -1) to get t = (u - v)/a.

probe.question: Make t the subject of v = u - at.

misconceptions.root_belief: minus signs can be ignored when they get in the way
misconceptions.source_hint: research on sign errors in solving linear equations

misconceptions.statement: The denominator can simply be dropped when rearranging a fraction formula.
misconceptions.why: Students think what is under the line is only a label for the division.
misconceptions.fix: The denominator must be cleared by multiplying both sides by it, so it appears on the other side.

probe.question: Make d the subject of s = d/t.

misconceptions.root_belief: what sits below the line does not matter

misconceptions.statement: When the subject is in the denominator, a/b and b/a give the same answer so the order does not matter.
misconceptions.why: Students overgeneralise that order does not matter in multiplication to division.
misconceptions.fix: Division is not commutative; if s = d/t then t = d/s, not s/d.

probe.question: Make t the subject of s = d/t.

misconceptions.root_belief: order does not matter in any operation
misconceptions.source_hint: research on commutativity wrongly applied to division

misconceptions.statement: If x appears in two terms, divide by each coefficient separately and add the results.
misconceptions.why: Students think division spreads over a sum on the denominator side too.
misconceptions.fix: Combine the terms first to (a + b)x, then divide by the whole bracket (a + b).

probe.question: Make x the subject of ax + bx = c.

misconceptions.root_belief: operations spread over addition in every position
misconceptions.source_hint: research on misuse of the distributive property in algebra

misconceptions.statement: The inverse of squaring is dividing by 2.
misconceptions.why: Students think squaring means doubling, so undoing it halves.
misconceptions.fix: Squaring means multiplying a number by itself, and it is undone by taking the square root.

probe.question: A = s². Find s when A = 36.

misconceptions.root_belief: a power means multiplying by the exponent
misconceptions.source_hint: research on squaring confused with doubling

misconceptions.statement: Taking the square root of both sides means taking the root of each term separately.
misconceptions.why: Students extend the rule that roots split over products to sums and differences.
misconceptions.fix: The square root applies to the whole side, so from c² - b² you get √(c² - b²), which is not c - b.

probe.question: Make a the subject of c² = a² + b².

misconceptions.root_belief: an operation splits over addition term by term
misconceptions.source_hint: research on the misconception that √(a²+b²) = a + b

misconceptions.statement: After taking a square root, both the positive and negative values are valid lengths.
misconceptions.why: Students learn ± for x² = 49 and apply it without thinking about the context.
misconceptions.fix: A radius or side is a length, so only the positive root is used in a geometry formula.

probe.question: Which values of radius satisfy πr² = 154?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule applies the same way in every context

misconceptions.statement: A square root gives only one value, so x² = 25 has just one solution.
misconceptions.why: Calculator square roots show only the positive value.
misconceptions.fix: In a pure equation x² = 25, both 5 and -5 satisfy it, though a physical length keeps only the positive one.

probe.question: Solve x² = 25 and give all values of x.

misconceptions.root_belief: a question has only one correct answer
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' handling of both roots in quadratic equations

misconceptions.statement: In πr² the square applies to π as well as r.
misconceptions.why: Students read the exponent as covering the whole term πr.
misconceptions.fix: The exponent 2 belongs only to r, so A = π × (r × r), and r = √(A/π).

probe.question: Make r the subject of A = πr².

misconceptions.root_belief: an exponent covers everything written before it
misconceptions.source_hint: research on scope of exponents, e.g. 2x² read as (2x)²

misconceptions.statement: You must always rearrange a formula first because substituting numbers first gives a wrong answer.
misconceptions.why: Teachers show rearranging first, so students believe it is the only valid order.
misconceptions.fix: Both orders are valid: substituting numbers first and then solving gives the same answer.

probe.question: Ria put v = 20, u = 5, t = 3 into v = u + at first and found a = 5. Is her answer right?
probe.wrong_answer: No, substituting before rearranging always gives a wrong answer.

misconceptions.root_belief: only one method order is allowed

misconceptions.statement: Units are just labels, so values in different units can be put into a formula together.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the numbers and treat units as decoration.
misconceptions.fix: All quantities must be in consistent units before substituting, such as metres with seconds.

probe.question: Find speed in m/s from s = d/t with d = 200 m and t = 2 min.

misconceptions.root_belief: numbers matter, units are only decoration
misconceptions.source_hint: research on unit neglect in physics and mathematics word problems
